narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 51.1% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the second decile, noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk that you might struggle with the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.30 worked in the opposite direction. It is slightly above the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction toward passing, helping to offset some of the concern. Your LSAT score of 36 similarly nudged the outcome toward success, though its positive effect was a bit weaker than the GPA’s.

Taken together, the model concluded that the negative impact of your third-year class standing outweighed the modest advantages from your grades and test score, resulting in a failure probability high enough to deny admission.

You should focus on strengthening your academic performance in the remaining law school years and consider retaking the LSAT if possible. Improving either of those areas would likely change the model’s assessment and improve your chances on a future application. (218 words)
